newsitem.title: HUNGARY: VW WIDENS LEAD ON FIAT IN C.EUROPE.
newsitem.headline: VW WIDENS LEAD ON FIAT IN C.EUROPE.

text.p: Note to readers: Reuters wants to provide the best possible coverage of the East European car market and would like to know if readers find this survey useful or if they have suggestions for improvements. Please contact Mary-Ellen Barker in London on ++44 171 542 7723 or Michael Roddy in Budapest on ++36 1 327 4041. E-mail Mary-Ellen.Barker@Reuters.com or Mike.Roddy@Reuters.com.
By Ryan Tutak
Volkswagen AG widened its lead in central Europe's booming new auto market in April, accelerating ahead of rivals Fiat SPA and Daewoo Group, according to a monthly Reuters survey.
"Volkswagen's product profile is clearly strengthening, and that has helped," Edmund Chew, head of British consultancy Auto Business Ltd, told Reuters.
"Meanwhile, Fiat is continuing to rely on some outdated models for sales in central Europe," Chew added. "And Daewoo might be overextending itself in the region."

VW, increasing its lead 122 percent from March, outsold Fiat 24,084 units to 19,060 units in countries in the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) -- the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
Daewoo, which has become CEFTA's clear third power by buying several state-owned automakers in the region, sold only 15,153 units in April, slipping from 17,210 units in March.

But Daewoo's position will strengthen in July, when CEFTA admits Romania, where Daewoo sold nearly 2,000 units a month in 1996 on the strength of its large factory there. In contrast, Fiat and VW each sold under 250 units in Romania all last year.
No other automaker sold over 7,000 units in CEFTA in April.
Trailing the Big Three of central Europe were PSA Peugeot Citroen selling 6,053 units, General Motors Corp selling 5,909 units, Renault SA selling 5,890 units and Ford Motor Co selling 5,104 units.
VW -- including the Audi, SEAT, Skoda and VW brands -- overtook Fiat at the end of 1996. The German automotive group has kept the lead except in February, when it fell behind the Italian automaker.
Fiat -- including Alfa Romeo, Fiat, Iveco, Lancia and several specialty brands -- had been the annual leader in CEFTA sales from the time the trade pact formed in 1993 until 1995.
The data, based on information that Reuters obtained from a variety of sources, include cars, minibuses, pickups, vans and other four-wheeled motor vehicles not over five tonnes in gross weight.

Overall, CEFTA sales growth remained below its all-time peak in 1996, when sales rose 39.5 percent to 842,577 units. But the market is still buoyant, expanding 23.2 percent to 91,902 units in April 1997 from 74,567 units in April 1996.

CEFTA continued to look dynamic compared to western Europe, where year-on-year sales rose only 9.3 percent in April 1997, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers Association, known by its French acronym ACEA.
VW has built its lead on a broad presence in the region.
The German automotive group still centers its CEFTA strategy upon Czech brand Skoda, but it also plans to assemble models from each of its brands throughout central Europe.
VW assembles SEATs and Skodas in Poland as well as VWs in Poland and Slovakia. By mid-1998, it plans to start assembling Audis in Hungary.
Fiat has focused more narrowly on CEFTA. It owns the region's biggest car factory in Poland, but it builds no vehicles elsewhere in central Europe.

The Italian conglomerate sells twice as many brands as VW in CEFTA. But many of these brands, such as Ferrari and Maserati, feature high-priced specialty cars that attract only a small number of customers.
As a result, Fiats accounted for 98.4 percent of the Italian group's sales in central Europe in March, while Skodas represented only 68.6 percent of VW's sales.
Daewoo, which plans to build over 500,000 vehicles a year in central Europe by 2000, has led a Korean blitz on the region in recent years that already has yielded stunning results.
In April, Korean automakers sold 16,739 units in five countries in central Europe, not far behind the 21,414 units they sold in 18 countries in western Europe, ACEA reported.
